subject: sampling from roads, shore lines, rivers, vantage points,

messages.subject: sampling from roads, shore lines, rivers, vantage points,
parts:
Dear List,

Please forgive me for the blatant self promotion of a paper, but I have=20
recently got one accepted that deals with the often overlooked issue of=20
using distance sampling with samplers (lines or points) laid along=20
features with respect to which the animals might respond to. This could=20
lead to potentially severely biased estimates, and it's often the case=20
that we see studies conducted say using roads as transects without=20
properly evaluating the effect of the distribution of the animals with=20
respect to the roads on the density estimates. Often questions on this=20
list hint to the fact that this was the case, but rarely the question is=20
about that particular fact. I argue that quite often that fact should be=20
more worrying than the question being asked.

The paper was written in what I hope to be a style sufficiently=20
appealing for practitioners. The reference is:

Marques, T. A.; Buckland, S. T.; Bispo, R. & Howland, B. Accounting for=20
animal density gradients using independent information in distance=20
sampling surveys Statistical Methods and Applications, 2013. DOI:=20
10.1007/s10260-012-0223-2

Abstract: Distance sampling is extensively used for estimating animal=20
density or abundance. Conventional methods assume that location of line=20
or point transects is random with respect to the animal population, yet=20
transects are often placed along linear features such as roads, rivers=20
or shorelines that do not randomly sample the study region, resulting in=20
biased estimates of abundance. If it is possible to collect additional=20
data that allow an animal density gradient with respect to the transects=20
to be modelled, we show how to extend the conventional distance sampling=20
likelihood to give asymptotically unbiased estimates of density for the=20
covered area. We illustrate the proposed methods using data for a=20
kangaroo population surveyed by line transects laid along tracks, for=20
which the true density is known from an independent source, and the=20
density gradient with respect to the tracks is estimated from a sample=20
of GPS collared animals. For this example, density of animals increases=20
with distance from the tracks, so that detection probability is=20
overestimated and density underestimated if the non-random location of=20
transects is ignored. When we account for the density gradient, there is=20
no evidence of bias in the abundance estimate. We end with a list of=20
practical recommendations to investigators conducting distance sampling=20
surveys where density gradients could be an issue.

(pdf naturally available upon request)

I take the opportunity to ask everyone publishing distance sampling=20
related papers to send me their references (bibtex format preferred!),=20
to be added to the distance sampling reference web page hosted at:

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancesamplingreferences/

all the best,

Tiago
